title: More cadets, more money, less training: Military defends controversial suspension
summary: The second-in-command of Canada's military stood behind the decision to suspend most cadet training in various parts of the country, suggesting the program is swamped by an increase in participation…

image.caption: Cadets march in a parade following a Remembrance Day ceremony near CFB Gagetown in Oromocto, N.B., on Nov. 11. Most cadet training has been suspended across the country. (Darren Calabrese/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New

The second-in-command of Canada's military stood behind the decision to suspend most cadet training in various parts of the country, suggesting the program is swamped by an increase in participation and struggling not to blow its annual budget.
Military admits spending miscalculation forced suspension of popular youth activities

Vice-Admiral Angus Topshee, the vice chief of the defence staff who is responsible for the day-to-day operations of the military, testified Thursday before the House of Commons public accounts committee.

A set of leaked emails obtained by a number of media outlets, including CBC News, show weekend training and participation in competitions by cadets has been halted until the end of the fiscal year in March. Mandatory weekly parade nights, however, will continue at least for the time being.
Topshee told the tri-party committee that membership in the cadets program has jumped by roughly 20,000 in the last few years and funding for the program has increased to $265 million annually.
Vice-Admiral Angus Topshee prepares to appear before a standing committee on Parliament Hill Thursday. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)
"Unfortunately, a lot of the cadet funding is front-loaded. It happens during the summer months," Topshee said.
"And so they spent a large part of that expanded budget on summer training. And we didn't factor in the sizable increase in the number of cadets participating in the program."
The answer to questions from Conservative MP William Stevenson represent the clearest explanation to date from the military about the reason for the decision, which has angered many Canadians.

A written statement from the Department of National Defence (DND) late Wednesday referenced the increased participation and the higher budget, but focused on the fact that both the cadet and junior ranger programs were being reviewed.

items: Cadets being told to stand down as Canada adds billions to defence

blocks.text: Topshee added more clarity to the military position.
"Despite the fact the budget has grown, they have run up against a hard cap on the amount of money that they've been given," Topshee said.

"They are now on track to exceed that and they are living within their means, as all of us within the Department of Defence are," he added. "We are required to live within the budget we've been given and they spent theirs a little bit faster than they were intended to."
The written statement from the department implied that it was too early to say what "the full extent of any changes" would be because of the ongoing review.
Canadian Armed Forces pauses most cadet training over budget constraints
Deputy Minister of Defence Christiane Fox told the same committee that she supports the restoration of the training that has been put on pause.
"It is an essential program, not just for the military and the forces, it is an essential program for young Canadians to develop confidence, leadership, skill sets that we need," Fox said.
The decision to rein in the cadet program budget is just one part of a series of internal belt-tightening measures at DND.

Prime Minister Mark Carney's government has drastically ramped up defence spending and has largely exempted the department from its expenditure review program. But it has not entirely escaped the fiscal axe.

blocks.text: DND has been told to focus its billions of dollars in new investment on priority areas, including the purchase of new equipment.
At the same time, it is still subject to reductions planned in a previous federal budget, passed by the Trudeau government.
Those reductions in operations and maintenance funding continue to roll out this year with DND expected to find $459 million in savings this year.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Murray Brewster is the senior defence writer for CBC News, based in Ottawa. He has covered the Canadian military and foreign policy from Parliament Hill for over a decade. Among other assignments, he spent a total of 15 months on the ground covering the Afghan war for The Canadian Press. Prior to that, he covered defence issues and politics for CP in Nova Scotia for 11 years and was bureau chief for Standard Broadcast News in Ottawa.
